title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the prevalence of cocaine-induced psychosis in cocaine users

claims.statement: In people with lifetime cocaine use seen in treatment settings (17 studies, 5286 people, almost all in outpatient drug treatment services, with one inpatient service and one psychiatric emergency unit; 13 of all 20 included studies from the USA, 4 from Spain and one each from Canada, Brazil and the French Caribbean; mean age 37, 68% men; people with primary psychotic disorders excluded), one meta-analysis of studies published to August 2020 found that how common cocaine-induced psychosis is depends on how it is defined (Sabe et al., 2021). In 13 studies that asked about psychotic symptoms with cocaine (questionnaires such as the Cocaine Experience Questionnaire, which mainly asks about paranoia and also about hallucinations, or study-specific questions, in two studies a single symptom), a pooled 68.4% (95% CI 62.8 to 73.5; I² 89%) reported having had them; in 4 studies that used diagnostic interviews (PRISM or MINI) for a DSM cocaine-induced psychotic disorder, 16% (10.6 to 23.2; I² 89%; 8.5 to 28.3 with a between-study variance estimated within that subgroup alone, editors' calculation) met the criteria; by instrument the figures ranged from 11.7% (PRISM, 3 studies) to 84.2% (SAPS-CIP, 1 study), and by region from 25.1% in Europe to 66.5% in North America. The single pooled lifetime figure of 55.6% combines these definitions (I² 97%), and its printed interval (50.2 to 61.0) is narrower than a standard random-effects interval (46.0 to 64.8; editors' calculation). The figure for current use (50.2%, 32.0 to 68.4) rests on 102 people in three studies, two of them laboratory studies in which 12 of 28 and 29 of 44 volunteers reported paranoia while taking cocaine in a research unit and one a psychiatric emergency series (12 of 30), so it is not a prevalence among people who currently use cocaine. Other drug use was common where reported (lifetime dependence on alcohol 56.5% in 3 studies, cannabis 32% and opioids 30% in 2) and could not be separated from cocaine, and neither could amount or route; the authors state that cocaine cannot be shown to be directly responsible, that treatment samples may inflate the figures (selection and Berkson bias) while people's limited insight into their symptoms may deflate them, and that cross-sectional studies with mostly retrospective assessment cannot show cause. Two reports with identical counts may count the same 243 people twice (without one of them, 67.7% for symptoms, editors' calculation), and two studies, including the largest (2192 people), have no entry in the reference list. The review states, citing other work, that such symptoms are usually transient and pass with abstinence, and that a 2020 meta-analysis found no study of how often cocaine-induced psychotic disorder turns into schizophrenia; it did not measure either itself. A corrigendum to this review was published (Sabe et al., 2022, doi:10.1016/j.pnpbp.2021.110434) but has not been read, because the file saved under its name is a different document; it might correct the missing abstract, the reference list, the possibly duplicated study or the pooled figures themselves, so every figure here is provisional until it is read.
claims.magnitude: Lifetime, treatment samples: psychotic symptoms 68.4% (95% CI 62.8 to 73.5; 13 studies; I² 89%; prediction interval 47.8% to 83.6%, editors' calculation); DSM cocaine-induced psychotic disorder 16% (10.6 to 23.2; 4 studies; I² 89%; 8.5 to 28.3 with its own between-study variance, editors' calculation); both combined 55.6% (printed 50.2 to 61.0; standard random effects 46.0 to 64.8, prediction interval 18.7% to 87.2%, editors' calculation); by instrument 11.7% (PRISM) to 84.2% (SAPS-CIP); Europe 25.1%, North America 66.5%. Current use (3 studies, 102 people, mostly laboratory): 50.2% (32.0 to 68.4), not a population prevalence. Without the possibly duplicated study: symptoms 67.7% (62.1 to 72.9). All provisional until the corrigendum is read.
